chapter: Circus shows and learning to voice
title: The Chicago trade school and learning from Don Redman in New York
summary: He lived with Dr. Dorsey, worked at the lunch counter, learned musical terms at school, then in New York met Bingie Madison and Don Redman's six-part harmony.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: But when you stayed in Chicago, it was to go to this music college, was it?

Yeah, I went there, because my brother knew a doctor there named Dr. Dorsey, and I lived with Dr. Dorsey, he owned a drugstore. And then from -- I worked a little at the lunch counter and I would go down to this trade school. You'd work your way through it, and I worked in the bakery shop for awhile.
Well, what did you learn in this school?

A little bit more about -- well, I would say dynamics and correct wording for this and that, because they were using a lot of Latin terms, you know, like -- they was using a lot of Latin terms in music, like tempo and -- wait a minute, I forgot the words.
Poca tempo and all that stuff.

Yeah. So finally I got away from all that. And so that's what I learned there. It got so they couldn't offer me much and (unintelligible) what I got here, I got a foundation, so I went creating for myself. So when I came to New York, that's when I run into guys like Bingie Madison, who was voicing, and then ran into Don Redman, and Don Redman was doing six-part harmony, and that's when -- and when I heard his (unintelligible) I said, what do you name this chord? He says, it's just a double the minute. Nobody's even named it yet. You get that six part.
